children: The Federal Open Market Committee held its benchmark rate at 3.75%-4.00% on Wednesday, as widely expected, taking a breath after its rate hike in September.
Two committee members dissented — Fed Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack — preferring to raise the rate by 1/4 of a percentage point.
The committee continued to acknowledge that inflation remains too high but said the pause would provide more information to help it "determine the policy stance appropriate
to ensure a timely return of inflation to the committee's 2% goal."
The U.S. economy is "expanding at a strong pace," stronger language than its description of a “solid pace” in its September statement.

, Investing Group Leader for Retirement Income Warrior. "What's more, there was a new line in the statement regarding the Fed's need for 'the accumulation of more information to determine future policy.' I surmise they are referring to the PCE report out tomorrow and the midterm elections within a week."

The rest of the FOMC's economic assessment repeats the prior one. "While uncertainty remains elevated owing, in part, to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient," the FOMC said. "Productivity growth is strong, and capital investment is robust. Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little."
It also repeated that it's continuing its policy of maintaining ample reserves in the banking system.

Clark commented, "The bottom line is Fed's dual mandate of maximum employment and price stability remains central to its decision-making. The labor market is holding relatively firm while inflation remains sticky."

"This narrative gives the Fed latitude to maintain a restrictive monetary policy," he added. "Warsh will do his best to keep a hawkish tone during the press conference in an attempt to keep inflation under control. Further, with PCE out tomorrow and midterms less than a week away, this is standard practice for the Fed."
With the Fed's pass today on a rate hike, markets now see a higher probability of a 25-basis-point rate hike in December — to 86.0% from a 78.3% chance on Tuesday, according to the CME FedWatch tool.
